newsitem.title: USA: Cereal wars heat up -- again.
newsitem.headline: Cereal wars heat up -- again.

text.p: As in the automobile and computer business, cereal makers are learning that brand names given high-profile advertising aren't enough to hold on to their market share. They have to make the product grab the consumer, which mostly means cutting prices.
This means narrowing the gap between the most popular brands and the not-so-popular so that the latter aren't just being snapped due to price at the expense of the former.
Price cuts, it turns out once again, do work.

After they starting trimming prices in April, the big three cereal makers -- Kellogg Co., General Mills Corp., and Post Cereals, a division of the Kraft Foods unit of Philip Morris Cos. -- have enjoyed increased sales.

George Kress, an analyst at Argus Research Corp. in New York, said recently that the sales stimulus is so strong that it could raise this year's industry growth rate from the traditional 2 percent to 3 percent to 3 percent and over. That would be a meaningful change in an $8 billion industry.

The 20 percent lower prices of national brands have, as expected, also reduced the sales of store brand or private-label cereals, which makes sense since it was the rising sales of the lower-priced private brands that pushed brand-name makers into cutting prices in the first place.

As if the price churning isn't enough, a major shift in brand-name ownership and market share occurred Aug. 14 when General Mills, No. 2 to Kellogg, paid $330 million in stock to acquire the Chex and other cereal brands from Ralcorp Holdings in St. Louis.
This gave General Mills -- which makes Cheerios, Wheaties and Total cereals -- Ralcorp's Chex, Cookie Crisp, Almond Delight and other cereals to bolster its position.
The combination of the price cuts and the Chex acquisition have raised a number of likely changes involving brands and companies, industry experts say:
-- The Chex products will get a big push from General Mills, raising Chex's low profile to make it a major brand name. Chex prices will also be lowered soon.
-- If the present, healthier sales trend among the name-brand cereals isn't sustained, there will be another round of price cuts.

"National-brand cereals are only beginning to narrow the gap between them and private brands," said Gary Giblen, food analyst for Smith Barney. "This is just the beginning. Most retailers expect more price reductions."
-- Until then and perhaps even after, private cereal brands, which are prevalent at every major grocery chain, will continue to create an "implosion," as one source called it.

"It won't be enough for branded producers to explain away the cost of advertising to children on Saturday television as a reason for their higher prices," says Giblen. "Why should an 18-ounce package of corn flakes cost more than $2.50?"
Ralston's sale of its name brands, by the way, will leave it even more the kingpin of private-label cereals since it now can focus better on them.

Food retailers, while welcoming the price cuts, are a bit miffed at a companion move the name-brand cereal makers have made. The cereal makers have cut back discount-coupon programmes to soften the impact of the price cuts. For the consumer, the combination of price cuts and reduced coupon values surely will come as a bittersweet gift.

For Kellogg, whose Corn Flakes, Bran Flakes, Rice Krispies, Special K and other cereals make it the undisputed industry leader with a 35.7 percent market share against General Mills' pre-Chex share of 26.5 percent, the improved sales climate will come as a welcome relief.
In Battle Creek, Mich., Kellogg spokesman Anthony Hebron said the company does not comment on competitive moves or forecast its marketing strategy.
"We have 45 different types of cereals, but we have no plans for new products at this time," he said. "We have been focusing on strengthening our core business to give better value to our consumers."

In its second, fiscal quarter ended June 30, Kellogg was battered by the price reductions. Sales dropped to $1.65 billion against $1.78 billion in the same 1995 quarter while net income plummeted to $78.1 million, or 37 cents a share, from $1.35 billion, or 62 cents a share.
In the quarterly statement's comments, Kellogg Chairman Arnold Langbo said the results demonstrated "the impact of the price cuts and the competitive conditions in the U.S."

But he added, "The success of our continuing efforts to reduce costs throughout our global markets has enabled us to reduce prices in certain other markets. This action is consistent with our long-standing strategy of delivering more value to our consumers."
That price paring by Kellogg and the others -- Post was the first -- is clearly stimulating business.
"Sales of cereals since the price cuts have moved up more than moderately," said Michael Rourke of A&P in Montvale, N.J.,, one of the nation's biggest supermarket chains.
"But it has cut into the volume of private labels," Rourke added. "Overall, though, the entire category has moved up in sales."

Asked if he expected more price cuts, Rourke said he wasn't sure. "I don't know if it will happen when I read about rising prices of grain. I can't see a further cut in consumer prices until the commodity prices become stable or go down."

Nothing, it seems, is ever permanent or quite certain in the fiercely contested cereal business. The reality is that the real fight is between Kellogg and General Mills and it has been going on for about 15 years.

Nomi Ghez, food analyst at Goldman Sachs, sees the war continuing. "General Mills will definitely cut Chex's prices," she said. "The price cuts' only benefit is if it will stimulate the overall category. If it doesn't over a good period, we'll see another price war."
